caption_text: Fig. 1. Examples of potential harms related to AI systems. Trustworthy AI systems and their
description: Figure 1 illustrates three distinct categories of harm associated with Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems, presented as a horizontal flowchart from left to right. Each category is encapsulated in its own rounded rectangular box with a dark blue header bar containing white text: “Harm to People,” “Harm to an Organization,” and “Harm to an Ecosystem.” The boxes are connected by thin yellow-orange lines that span horizontally between them, visually indicating progression or relationship across the three domains. The content within each box is organized into bullet points using orange circular markers. --- **Left Box: Harm to People** - Individual: Harm to a person’s civil liberties, rights, physical or psychological safety, or economic opportunity. - Group/Community: Harm to a group such as discrimination against a population sub-group. - Societal: Harm to democratic participation or educational access. --- **Middle Box: Harm to an Organization** - Harm to an organization’s business operations. - Harm to an organization from security breaches or monetary loss. - Harm to an organization’s reputation. --- **Right Box: Harm to an Ecosystem** - Harm to interconnected and interdependent elements and resources. - Harm to the global financial system, supply chain, or interrelated systems. - Harm to natural resources, the environment, and planet. Below this figure is a caption in bold serif font: “Fig. 1. Examples of potential harms related to AI systems. Trustworthy AI systems and their responsible use can mitigate negative risks and contribute to benefits for people, organizations, and ecosystems.” --- **Section Context (Body Text Only)** Following the figure are two numbered sections from a larger document titled “NIST AI RMF 1.0” — specifically section **1.2 Challenges for AI Risk Management**, which discusses difficulties in measuring risks quantitatively or qualitatively due to poorly defined failures, and subsection **1.2.1 Risk Measurement**, detailing challenges related to third-party software/hardware/data integration, transparency of metrics, customer usage patterns, and tracking emergent risks. --- *Note: The physical page number “Page 5” appears at the bottom right corner.*

caption_text: Fig. 4. Characteristics of trustworthy AI systems. Valid & Reliable is a necessary condition of
description: Figure 4 depicts the characteristics of trustworthy AI systems, organized into two main groups with distinct spatial relationships and hierarchical structure. The top row contains five smaller blue boxes arranged horizontally from left to right: "Safe," "Secure & Resilient," "Explainable & Interpretable," "Privacy-Enhanced," and "Fair - With Harmful Bias Managed." These are positioned above a long, wide horizontal bar labeled "Valid & Reliable" that spans most of the width. To the far right stands an isolated vertical blue box containing two lines: "Accountable & Transparent." The caption below reads: Fig. 4. Characteristics of trustworthy AI systems. Valid & Reliable is a necessary condition of trustworthiness and is shown as the base for other trustworthiness characteristics. Accountable & Transparent is shown as a vertical box because it relates to all other characteristics.
